title: Northmere Food Safety Code overview | text: title: Northmere Food Safety Code overview
note: The Northmere Food Safety Code is the regulatory regime that governs how Brackenridge Provisions makes and ships chilled ready meals and soups. It sets out duties for hazard analysis, hygiene, allergen handling, record keeping and reporting. The code is enforced by the Northmere Food Standards Office, which can inspect without notice, request records and suspend a plant licence when serious failures are found.

title: Allergen management across both plants | text: title: Allergen management across both plants
note: Allergen management covers how Brackenridge stops the fourteen regulated allergens from ending up in products that do not declare them. It includes segregated storage, colour-coded utensils, production scheduling that runs allergen-free recipes first, validated cleaning between products and label checks at packing.

title: Does the chutney line qualify for the low-risk exemption? | text: title: Does the chutney line qualify for the low-risk exemption?
note: The chutney line makes high-acid, high-sugar products with a long ambient shelf life. These look like they meet the low-risk exemption conditions, but one recipe uses fresh garlic in oil, which may push it outside the definition. We need a ruling before claiming the exemption.

title: Recall execution playbook | text: title: Recall execution playbook
note: The recall execution playbook is the detailed guide the incident team follows once a decision has been made to withdraw or recall a Brackenridge product. It sits behind the shorter recall procedure and is written so that a capable person who has never run a recall could still follow it at three in the morning. It covers roles, communications, physical recovery of stock, regulator contact, and how the incident is closed.

The first hour is about stopping further harm. The technical manager confirms the affected product, batch codes and date range. Warehouse staff place an immediate hold on all matching stock still on site and in the third-party cold store. The logistics provider is asked to stop any deliveries in transit and return them. At the same time the incident team is assembled, usually the technical manager, the operations director, the commercial lead, the compliance lead and someone from customer service, with clear names written on the incident board against each role.

The second step is scoping the distribution. Using the traceability system, the compliance lead lists every customer who received affected stock, the quantity, the delivery date and the delivery point. For retail customers this often means hundreds of individual stores. The list is checked against the logistics provider's own delivery records because past exercises showed small discrepancies between our dispatch data and what was actually delivered.

The third step is regulator contact. The regulator is told what is known, what is being done and what is still uncertain. Drafts of the consumer notice and point-of-sale notice are shared for comment before they are published. The regulator may ask for changes in wording, and we generally accept them because a joint message travels further and attracts less criticism later.

The fourth step is customer notification. Most retail customers use a shared industry portal through which suppliers post withdrawal and recall notices, and their store systems then block the product at the till. Food service customers are contacted by phone and email by the commercial team using the recall contact tree. Every notification is logged with the time, the person contacted and the confirmation received. A customer is not considered notified until they have confirmed receipt.

Communications to the public are handled carefully. The consumer notice uses plain words, names the product, pack size, batch codes and dates exactly as printed, explains the risk without alarm, and tells people what to do. It is published on our website, shared with the regulator for their alert service and sent to any consumer media contacts the regulator recommends. Social media questions are answered with the same approved wording, and staff are reminded not to comment on the recall in a personal capacity. A single spokesperson, normally the operations director, handles any press calls, and every other person in the business refers questions to them rather than trying to help.

There is an important exception to portal notification. The Haverly Stores account must always be phoned directly, because their head office does not act on portal notices for suppliers of our size and will only accept a phone call to their product safety duty line, which is staffed until 22:00. If a recall starts later than that, the call is made at 06:00 the next morning and a written notice is emailed overnight so that it is waiting when their team arrives. This exception is written into our supply contract with them.

Recovery and reconciliation follow. Returned stock is counted, compared with the quantity dispatched and destroyed under supervision with a destruction certificate. The recovery rate is tracked daily. When the rate stops rising and the regulator agrees, the incident is closed. A review meeting is held within two weeks to capture lessons, and any changes to the playbook or contact tree are made before the next mock recall.

title: CAPA tracker register | text: title: CAPA tracker register
note: The CAPA tracker is the shared register of every open corrective and preventive action, its source, owner, due date and evidence of closure. It is reviewed weekly by plant managers and quarterly by the compliance committee. Overdue items are highlighted automatically.

title: Tallyport product overview | text: title: Tallyport product overview
note: Tallyport is the field service scheduling and invoicing product built by Corvane Software. Office staff use the web app to schedule jobs and raise invoices, and technicians use the mobile app to see their day, record work, capture signatures and take payments. The delivery team is about forty engineers split into five squads.

title: Feature flag cleanup | text: title: Feature flag cleanup
note: Feature flag cleanup is the routine removal of flags, and the code behind the dead branch, once a feature is fully rolled out or abandoned. A small script lists flags that have been fully on or fully off for more than a month and opens tickets for the owning squad.

title: Migrations backward compatible for one release | text: title: Migrations backward compatible for one release
note: Every schema change must work with both the current and the previous version of the application, because during a rollout both versions run at once and a rollback may be needed. Destructive changes such as dropping a column wait at least one release.

title: Alert noise hides real problems | text: title: Alert noise hides real problems
note: Many alerts fire for conditions that fix themselves or need no action. Engineers start ignoring them, and a real problem can sit unnoticed among dozens of noisy notifications.

title: App store review delays hotfix | text: title: App store review delays hotfix
note: An urgent fix for the mobile app cannot reach users until it passes store review, which can take anywhere from hours to several days. During that time technicians remain on the broken version.

title: Wrenfold Studio workshop practice | text: title: Wrenfold Studio workshop practice
note: Wrenfold Studio is a small design consultancy that runs hands-on workshops for client organisations, mostly councils, charities and mid-sized service businesses. A typical engagement mixes discovery workshops, user research, prototyping and a final readout. The studio has six designers and two researchers, and every workshop has a lead facilitator and a supporting facilitator.

title: Internal design critique sessions | text: title: Internal design critique sessions
note: A design critique is a structured session where designers show work in progress and colleagues give feedback against the goals of the work. Critique is about improving the design, not judging the designer. Wrenfold holds internal critiques twice a week.

title: Post-workshop participant survey | text: title: Post-workshop participant survey
note: The post-workshop survey is a five-question form sent within a day of each workshop. It asks how useful the day was, which activity worked best, which worked least, whether people felt heard and what they would change.

title: Think aloud protocol briefed with a practice task | text: title: Think aloud protocol briefed with a practice task
note: Before the first real task in a usability session, participants practise thinking aloud on an unrelated simple activity, such as finding a recipe on a website. This warms them up and lets the moderator correct the habit of going silent.

title: Workshop materials available in large print | text: title: Workshop materials available in large print
note: Handouts, templates and agendas for every in-person workshop must be available in large print on request, and at least two large print copies are brought to every session whether or not anyone has asked.

title: Customer call notes overview | text: title: Customer call notes overview
note: Customer call notes record conversations between Corvane's customer success team and Tallyport customers. Notes capture who was on the call, what they raised, what we promised and any follow-up. They are the shared memory of each account, so that anyone picking it up can see the history without asking around.

title: Darnley Clinics complaint about invoice PDF layout | text: title: Darnley Clinics complaint about invoice PDF layout
note: Darnley's billing team complained that invoices to one insurer cut off the treatment code column when there are more than six lines. The insurer rejects invoices with missing codes, delaying payment. Support reproduced the issue and passed it to the billing squad.

title: Tolland Facilities contact prefers video calls | text: title: Tolland Facilities contact prefers video calls
note: Tolland's head of operations prefers video calls with cameras on and finds phone calls impersonal. He likes a short agenda shared an hour before and a recording made available afterwards for colleagues who could not attend.

title: Outage communication complaints | text: title: Outage communication complaints
note: After recent outages, several customers said the hardest part was not knowing what was happening. They found the status page slow to update and support agents unable to give an estimate. Many said honest uncertainty would be better than silence.

title: Who should be invited to the advisory board? | text: title: Who should be invited to the advisory board?
note: The advisory board currently has mostly large accounts. Should we invite smaller customers too, so that their needs are heard, even though they bring less revenue?
